candidate.blueprint_locator: Printed p.7, Management of Care — manage care to meet client needs, use organizational resources appropriately, collaborate and supervise within care-delivery systems
candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — nurse-manager span of control and workload design
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize nurse-manager span of control as a multidimensional workload-design decision that should account for unit, staff, manager, and organizational factors rather than direct-report count alone.

options.A: Because an appropriate span depends on unit, staff, organizational, and manager factors; an excessively broad span can create an unmanageable workload and is associated with worse workforce and some patient-safety outcomes.
options.B: Because span of control affects payroll only and has no meaningful relationship to manager workload, staff outcomes, or patient-care outcomes.
options.C: Because the largest possible span always improves supervision by allowing one manager to standardize every clinical and staffing decision.
options.D: Because patient acuity, unit complexity, staff skill and stability, and manager experience should be excluded when managerial workload is designed.

candidate.rationale: Recent nursing-management research supports treating span of control as more than a simple headcount. A 2024 Delphi study identified determinants involving unit complexity, resource management, staff number/stability/skill mix, manager experience and autonomy, and organizational factors. A 2026 multisite study found wide variation in nurse-manager span and reported associations between larger span measures and nurse turnover and falls, concluding that manageable workloads may improve workforce and patient outcomes. A is therefore the best answer. B through D ignore the multidimensional nature and documented outcome associations.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Nurse-manager span of control is influenced by multiple unit, staff, manager, and organizational factors; broader span measures have been associated with nurse turnover and fall outcomes, supporting manageable rather than maximized workloads.
candidate.source_document_title: Impact of Nurse Manager Span-of-Control on Turnover and Patient Safety in Acute Care; Determinants of First-Line Nurse Managers' Span of Control: A Delphi Study
candidate.source_locator: 2026 article Abstract — Objective/Results/Conclusions; 2024 Delphi article Abstract — Results identifying unit, professional, first-line nurse manager, and organization determinant categories
candidate.source_organization: Peer-reviewed nursing-management research indexed by U.S. National Library of Medicine (PubMed)
candidate.stem: Why should a health system avoid setting a nurse manager's span of control solely by maximizing the number of direct reports?
